subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: Folawns is a combined salon and medical spa, and the homepage handles that split well: the hero offers two separate buttons — “Book Salon Appointment” and “Book Med Spa Appointment” — so a visitor is never routed toward the wrong calendar. The full desktop navigation (Home, Specials, Service Menu, Shop, More) is also shown openly rather than hidden behind a hamburger icon, and “A Legacy of Exceptional Care Since 1994” is a genuine, specific longevity signal most practices in this review set cannot make.

Two things are missing from the opening screen on both devices: a phone number or address, and any named person behind the medical treatments. The homepage text describes injectables, lasers and facials as “backed by science,” but no practitioner, medical director or credential appears anywhere in the captured page content. For treatments that require a needle, that is the question a full-fee patient asks first.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the opening screen of the homepage on desktop and mobile, plus the site's own text as far as it was captured (the extract is truncated partway through the services section). Treatment pages, the full page below the fold, and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. No traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Booking clarity and visible navigation hold the score up. What is missing is almost entirely about proof: no name attached to the medical treatments, and no phone number or address on the first screen of either device.

scorecard.finding: A real photo of the building and two clear booking paths, but a generic headline with no location named.
“Since 1994” is a genuine signal; no practitioner or credential is named anywhere.
Salon and med spa booking are kept separate — a real, specific strength.
Clear defaults on where to book; no visible proof near the decision.
Sticky Phone / Email / Book Now bar; no number shown as readable text.
No address, phone number or city visible on the opening screen.

strengthsLead: For a two-business site, the homepage does the hardest part — keeping salon and medical visitors apart — correctly.

strengths.title: Two separate booking buttons, not one.
strengths.body: “Book Salon Appointment” and “Book Med Spa Appointment” sit side by side in the hero. A visitor who wants a blowout is never one misclick away from a medical intake form, and the reverse is also true.

strengths.title: “A Legacy of Exceptional Care Since 1994.”
strengths.body: Over thirty years in business is stated plainly, in those words, on the homepage. Longevity is hard to fake and this practice has simply said it.

strengths.title: The full navigation is visible on desktop.
strengths.body: Home, Specials, Service Menu, Shop and More are all shown in the header rather than collapsed behind a hamburger icon — a visitor can see the whole site's shape immediately.

strengths.title: A concrete new-guest offer, with its own button.
strengths.body: “$20 off your first hair appointment & $100 off your first advanced facial, injectable or laser treatment” is a specific, stated number behind a “Claim Your New Guest Offer” CTA — not a vague “special offers” link.

captionDesktop: Desktop. The hero is a real photograph of the Folawns building with two script-style booking buttons; no phone number, address or city is visible on this screen.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. A sticky footer bar offers Phone, Email and Book Now as icons; no phone number appears as readable text anywhere on the captured screen.

findings.heading: No phone number, address or city appears on the opening screen of either device.
findings.evidence: On both the desktop and mobile captures, the hero carries the headline “Your goals. Our guidance. Your most radiant you yet.”, an italic subheading, and the two booking buttons — no telephone number, street address or city name is visible. The mobile sticky footer offers a “Phone” icon but no number is shown as text next to it.
findings.why: Proximity is usually the first filter a patient applies to a spa or med spa search, and a phone number a visitor can read builds more confidence than one hidden behind a tap. As captured, a visitor cannot confirm this is in San Antonio, or see the number before deciding whether to call.
findings.recommended: Add the city and a readable, tap-to-call phone number to the header or hero, in addition to the existing Phone icon.

findings.heading: No practitioner or credential is named anywhere in the captured homepage text.
findings.evidence: The site's own description states the medical treatments are “backed by science,” and the homepage text covers the hero, the new-guest offer, and the “Legacy of Exceptional Care Since 1994” section through into the start of the services list — at no point in that captured text does a name, title or credential appear.
findings.why: Injectables, lasers and other medical-spa treatments are decisions about a specific person's hands. Without a name attached, “backed by science” is a claim with no one standing behind it on the page a first-time patient actually lands on.
findings.recommended: Name the medical director or lead injector near the “Book Med Spa Appointment” button, and link through to the “Meet The Team” page already in the header menu.

findings.heading: Both booking buttons are set in a decorative script font.
findings.evidence: “Book Salon Appointment” and “Book Med Spa Appointment” are rendered in a hand-written-style script on a gold background, at a similar visual weight to the italic subheading above them.
findings.why: These two buttons carry the single most important decision on the page — which calendar to open. A script face is the hardest common font style to read at speed, adding a small tax to the words that most need to be scanned instantly.
findings.recommended: Keep the brand styling, but confirm the button text is legible at a glance on a real phone, or increase weight/size for those two labels specifically.

findings.heading: Four separate action buttons appear before any service information is given.
findings.evidence: The header shows “BOOK ONLINE” and “SHOP GIFT CARDS” as outlined buttons; the hero beneath adds “Book Salon Appointment” and “Book Med Spa Appointment”. All four are visible without scrolling on desktop.
findings.why: The salon/med spa split is a genuine strength, but “Book Online” in the header does not obviously differ from the two hero buttons beneath it, and a visitor is asked to choose between four buttons before reading what either business actually offers.
findings.recommended: Consider whether the header's “Book Online” button is still needed once the hero offers both specific booking paths, or point it to the same choice rather than a third path.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: The visible top navigation and standard header layout match what most visitors already expect.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Both booking buttons are large and easy to tap on mobile; the sticky Phone/Email/Book Now bar keeps them reachable while scrolling.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No name, credential or address sits near either booking button — the two places a hesitant patient is most likely to look.
“Backed by science” is stated, but no practitioner name or credential is attached to it anywhere in the captured page.
Strong: two clearly labelled paths (salon vs. med spa) rather than one generic button.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: The stated new-guest offer ($20 off hair, $100 off an advanced facial/injectable/laser treatment) gives a first-time visitor a concrete reason to pick a first service.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: The copy stays modest — “Since 1994” and a stated discount read as facts rather than overclaiming.

roadmap.actions: Add a readable phone number and “San Antonio” to the header or hero. Review whether the header's “Book Online” button duplicates the two hero booking buttons.

Name the medical director or lead injector beside the “Book Med Spa Appointment” button and link to the existing “Meet The Team” page. Confirm the script-font buttons are legible at real device sizes.

Build out credential and team detail under the named practitioner. Assess treatment-page depth (not covered by this review). Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above can be replaced with the practice's own numbers.

limitations: This review assessed the opening screen of the homepage at desktop and 390 pixels wide, together with the site's own text as far as it was captured — that text extract is truncated partway through the services section, so any content further down the homepage or on other pages was not reviewed. Treatment-page depth, the full booking flow and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
